newsitem.title: USA: Mega-alliances seen as future of air competition.
newsitem.headline: Mega-alliances seen as future of air competition.

text.p: Mega-alliances involving several international airlines will dominate the future of the airline industry, leaving "unmarried" carriers to flounder, airline experts said.

"Competition is now heading towards alliance network versus alliance network, instead of individual airline versus airline," Cyril Murphy, vice president of international affairs for UAL Corp's United Airlines, said at the Sixth Annual Phoenix International Aviation Symposium.

Industry executives cited a potential link between AMR Corp's American Airlines, British Airways Plc and Japan Airlines Co Ltd as an example of global heavyweights combining forces to dominate the major international routes.

American, the second largest carrier in the United States, has a stronghold in Miami, which is a key gateway to Latin America. To combine American's presence in the U.S. and Latin American with BA's strength in London and JAL's dominance in Tokyo would create "an almost impregnable alliance since they will dominate the main, unique superhubs," Murphy said.
"It's not that we fear this alliance, it's that we fear for the consumers," Murphy said.

Anthony Fortnam, BA's vice president of government and international affairs, declined to comment on whether BA will seek to add a third airline its proposed alliance with American. Fortnam said BA's main focus remains finalizing its proposed pact with American.

Mega-alliances will allow carriers to benefit from their partners' strong brand identity and route structure, giving the partners a seamless global network with fewer regulatory restrictions. Alliances also spare airlines the cost of building its own presence and facilities in foreign countries.

Critics suggest mega-alliances will kill competition. This would force air fares higher and service quality lower. The shift towards global alliances also would weed out smaller, independent carriers, several industry experts said.

"Airlines that don't get involved in (a) mega-alliance will be at a disadvantage. They will have difficulty competing and will be relegated to niche players," said Timothy Hannegan, assistant director, U.S. General Accounting Office.

"Five or six years from now, carriers that aren't part of an alliance who still try to compete on a global basis will be clobbered," said Joel Spiro, deputy assistant secretary for transportation affairs for the U.S. Department of State.
Regulators, however, may move slowly in approving alliances that give a few carriers dominance on the major internation routes.
"At the end of the day, we'll see four or five mega-alliances. But getting from here to there will be difficult," Hannegan said.
